content:
UK Mountain Pass Rankings for Motorcyclists

Mountain passes are the purest expression of motorcycle road riding. The climb, the hairpins, the summit, the descent — each pass is a complete experience. Britain's mountains may not match the Alps for sheer altitude, but they deliver passes of extraordinary character and drama. Here are the best, ranked for riding quality.

1. Bealach na Bà (Applecross Pass), Scotland

Height: 626m (2,054ft) | Gradient: Up to 20% | Rating: ★★★★★

The undisputed king of UK passes. Alpine-style hairpins, vertiginous drops, and a summit panorama stretching to the Outer Hebrides. Nothing else in Britain comes close to this combination of engineering and landscape.

2. Hardknott Pass, Lake District

Height: 393m (1,289ft) | Gradient: Up to 33% | Rating: ★★★★★

Britain's steepest road pass. The gradient is ferocious, the hairpins are tight, and the views across Eskdale are magnificent. Add the Roman fort at the summit and you have a pass that combines challenge, history, and beauty.

3. A4069 Black Mountain Pass, Wales

Height: 493m (1,617ft) | Gradient: Up to 15% | Rating: ★★★★★

The finest riding pass in Wales. Wide enough for confident riding, sweeping enough for flow, and remote enough to feel wild. The southern descent is one of the most enjoyable pieces of road in Britain.

4. Llanberis Pass (A4086), Snowdonia

Height: 359m (1,178ft) | Gradient: Moderate | Rating: ★★★★

Dramatic mountain scenery at its most intense. The road climbs between towering crags with Snowdon's east face looming above. Technical and atmospheric.

5. Wrynose Pass, Lake District

Height: 393m (1,289ft) | Gradient: Up to 25% | Rating: ★★★★

The partner to Hardknott, often ridden in combination. Less extreme than Hardknott but still demanding, with wonderful views down into Little Langdale.

6. Horseshoe Pass (A542), North Wales

Height: 417m (1,367ft) | Gradient: Moderate | Rating: ★★★★

A classic sweeping pass through limestone scenery above the Vale of Llangollen. Well-surfaced and flowing — a rider's road.

7. Cairn o' Mount (B974), Aberdeenshire

Height: 455m (1,488ft) | Gradient: Moderate | Rating: ★★★★

An ancient route over the Mounth, connecting Deeside to the coast. The summit views are vast and the road is fast and flowing.

8. Honister Pass, Lake District

Height: 356m (1,167ft) | Gradient: Up to 25% | Rating: ★★★★

Steep, narrow, and spectacular, connecting Borrowdale to Buttermere through the slate quarries.

9. Gospel Pass, Black Mountains, Wales

Height: 549m (1,801ft) | Gradient: Moderate | Rating: ★★★★

The highest road pass in Wales. Quiet, remote, and beautiful — a hidden gem in the Black Mountains above Hay-on-Wye.

10. Kirkstone Pass, Lake District

Height: 454m (1,489ft) | Gradient: Up to 20% | Rating: ★★★

The highest pass in the Lake District on a public road. The Kirkstone Pass Inn at the summit has been serving travellers since the 1400s.

UK passes are short compared to Alpine monsters, but they pack enormous drama into their brief climbs. Many can be linked together in a single day — try Hardknott + Wrynose + Honister + Kirkstone for a Lake District pass marathon.

Tips for Riding UK Passes

  • Ride early morning for empty roads — passes attract tourist traffic from mid-morning
  • Use a lower gear than you think you need on descents — engine braking saves your brakes
  • Watch for wet surfaces at altitude — mountain passes often have standing water or damp patches
  • Livestock on mountain roads is common — slow down and be patient
  • Temperature drops significantly at altitude — dress warmer than the valley suggests

Accommodation and Dining

Lyme Regis, Weymouth, and Swanage all make excellent overnight stops. The Seaside Boarding House in Burton Bradstock combines boutique comfort with a cliff-top location overlooking Chesil Beach. For camping, Eweleaze Farm near Osmington opens for just four weeks in summer and offers camping directly on a private cliff-top meadow above the sea. The Anchor Inn at Seatown serves fresh Dorset seafood with views across Lyme Bay — one of the finest pub locations on the south coast. West Bay's harbour has excellent fish and chip shops, and the Hive Beach Café at Burton Bradstock serves locally caught crab and mackerel that touring riders rate among the best seaside food in England.

Touring Tips for Cornwall

Cornwall is narrow — the widest point is only 45 miles from north to south coast. This means you can ride from Atlantic surf to sheltered harbour in under an hour. Plan figure-of-eight routes that cover both coasts in a day. Accommodation in summer needs booking well in advance — Cornwall is Britain's most popular holiday destination. Campsites like South Penquite Farm on Bodmin Moor and Trevalgan Touring Park near St Ives offer great biker-friendly facilities. For food beyond pasties, try the Gurnard's Head gastropub between St Ives and Zennor — locally sourced food in a wild clifftop setting. The Ship Inn at Mawgan Porth and the Rashleigh Inn at Polkerris both serve excellent seafood with harbour or beach views.

Planning Your Pembrokeshire Tour

Pembrokeshire is compact enough for a long weekend tour. Base yourself in Tenby, St David's, or Fishguard and explore by day ride. Accommodation ranges from clifftop campsites (Caerfai Farm near St David's is spectacular) to boutique B&Bs in Tenby and Newport. For food, the Shed in Porthgain serves fresh fish in a converted fisherman's warehouse — a unique and excellent stop. The Griffin Inn in Dale is a proper sailing pub with harbour views and good food. And the Celtic Corner café in St David's serves possibly the best coffee in Pembrokeshire. Fuel is available in all main towns, and the distances are short enough that range is never a concern. The B roads through the interior are quiet and pleasant, connecting the dramatic coastal sections.
keyTakeaways: The Bealach na Ba (2,054ft) tops the rankings for its Alpine hairpins and Outer Hebrides panorama.
Hardknott is Britain's steepest road pass at up to 33%, with the Roman fort at its summit.
The A4069 Black Mountain Pass is the finest riding pass in Wales, wide and flowing.
Lake District passes such as Hardknott, Wrynose, Honister, and Kirkstone can be linked in a single day.
Ride early for empty roads, use engine braking on descents, and dress warmer than the valley suggests.

faq.q: Which is the single best UK pass for a motorcyclist?
faq.a: The Bealach na Ba in Wester Ross is the standout. Nothing else in Britain matches its combination of genuine Alpine-style hairpins, vertiginous drops, and a summit panorama stretching to the Outer Hebrides. It demands respect for its gradients and single-track width, but ridden on a dry, quiet morning it is the closest thing to Alpine riding the UK offers.

faq.q: Can I ride several Lake District passes in one day?
faq.a: Yes, and it makes a superb day. A classic circuit links Hardknott, Wrynose, Honister, and Kirkstone, packing enormous drama into a compact area. Start early to beat tourist traffic, because these narrow passes clog badly by mid-morning. Give yourself recovery time, as the constant steep hairpins and hill starts are physically and mentally demanding.

faq.q: How should I ride the steep descents safely?
faq.a: Select a lower gear than you think you need and let engine braking do the work, rather than dragging the brakes until they fade or lock. On passes like Hardknott and Honister the gradient is relentless, so set your speed early and keep it steady. Watch for damp patches, gravel, and oncoming traffic drifting wide on blind hairpins.

faq.q: What should I wear given the altitude?
faq.a: Dress warmer than the valley weather suggests, because temperature drops noticeably with height and summit car parks are exposed and windy. A summit can be several degrees colder than the base, and mountain passes often hold standing water or damp patches long after lower roads dry. Layers you can add at the top keep you comfortable and sharp.
